claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, corresponding to approximately 20 at.% of each element.
A combinatorial synthesis method can create a spatial composition gradient in HfNbTaTiZr.
Arc melting is an established synthesis method for high-entropy alloys.
Arc melting or additive manufacturing can be used to generate a controlled spatial composition gradient while holding other processing conditions constant.
Systematically changing elemental percentages and correlating local composition, microstructure, and mechanical measurements can be used to study constituent effects.
Changing constituent ratios in HfNbTaTiZr produces local variations in lattice strain and atomic-size mismatch.
Changing constituent ratios in HfNbTaTiZr affects phase stability.
Hf is a relatively large-atomic-radius constituent of HfNbTaTiZr.
Increasing the fraction of larger-radius elements increases lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and increases solid-solution strengthening.
Increasing the Hf fraction in HfNbTaTiZr will increase hardness relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Increasing the Hf fraction in HfNbTaTiZr will increase yield strength relative to the equiatomic baseline.
The strength and hardness increases caused by greater large-element content may be accompanied by reduced ductility.
The predicted compositional effects apply only when processing and microstructural conditions are held constant.
Nanoindentation and micro-compression or tensile testing can map local hardness and yield strength along the composition gradient.
Failure to observe the predicted positive correlation, or any statistically significant mechanical-property variation, would falsify the hypothesis.
